source_evidence.anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup and Algorithm 1
source_evidence.observation: The standing setup takes A in R^(m x n), m >= n, with rank(A) = n. It defines A = (a_1,...,a_n), Q = (q_1,...,q_n), and R = (r_jk). Standard CGS-S computes r_kk = ||v_k||_2.

CGS-P computes s_k = Q_(k-1)^T a_k, v_k = a_k - Q_(k-1)s_k, psi_k = ||a_k||_2, phi_k = ||s_k||_2, and r_kk = (psi_k - phi_k)^(1/2)(psi_k + phi_k)^(1/2). The page assumes IEEE floating-point arithmetic, states fl(x+y) = (x+y)(1+delta), |delta| <= epsilon_M for normalized-range results, and adopts a first-order approximation that neglects O(epsilon_M^2).

For every prefix k, Theorem 1 assumes c_4(m,k) epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1 and, to within O(epsilon_M^2), states the selected bound ||I - Q_k^T Q_k||_2 <= c_4(m,k) kappa_2(R_k)^2 epsilon_M. The enclosing theorem also states the residual, normal-equations, norm-comparison, and ||Q_k||_2 bounds in equations (4), (5), (6), and (8).
If A does not satisfy Theorem 1's assumptions, phi_k >= psi_k can occur and Algorithm 2 can break down, producing Q and R that are not real matrices.

The appendix treats psi_k and phi_k as computed norms via fl(||a_k||_2) and fl(||s_k||_2). It says condition (3) makes R nonsingular and r_kk > 0, and that r_kk > 0 in Algorithm 2 is possible only when psi_k > phi_k.

The proof uses Q_k = (A_k + Delta A_k)R_k^(-1) and the exact identity I - Q_k^T Q_k = R_k^(-T)(E_k - A_k^T Delta A_k - (Delta A_k)^T A_k - (Delta A_k)^T Delta A_k)R_k^(-1). Applying equations (4)-(6) yields c_4(m,k)||R_k||_2^2||R_k^(-1)||_2^2 epsilon_M + O(epsilon_M^2).

binders: Matrix dimensions m and n with m >= n, and a real input matrix A in R^(m x n). [PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup]
A floating-point machine unit epsilon_M and the matrices Q and R computed from A by Algorithm 2, CGS-P. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1]

For each k in {1,...,n}, A_k is the first k columns of A, while Q_k and R_k are the corresponding computed algorithm prefixes, with dimensions m x k and k x k respectively. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: algorithm block structure; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: definition of A_k and Theorem 1]
hypotheses: Inherited standing assumption: rank(A) = n, so A has full column rank. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup]
The computation is performed by Algorithm 2, the Cholesky-like or pythagorean classical Gram-Schmidt algorithm CGS-P. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2]
For every k = 1,...,n, the computed prefix R_k satisfies the strict condition c_4(m,k) epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (3)]

The floating-point setting is IEEE arithmetic, with the displayed relative-error model restricted to results in the normalized range and with second-order terms neglected. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: floating-point model and linear approximation]
conclusions: For every k = 1,...,n, to within terms of O(epsilon_M^2), the computed Q_k satisfies ||I - Q_k^T Q_k||_2 <= c_4(m,k) kappa_2(R_k)^2 epsilon_M, where I is dimensionally the k x k identity. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (7)]
definitions_and_conventions: A = (a_1,...,a_n), Q = (q_1,...,q_n), and R = (r_jk); the algorithms construct their prefixes column by column. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: notational conventions and algorithm setup]
kappa_2(R_k) is defined as ||R_k||_2 ||R_k^(-1)||_2. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: definition immediately before Theorem 1]
The companion quantities used in the proof are defined by Q_kR_k - A_k = Delta A_k and R_k^T R_k - A_k^T A_k = E_k. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equations (4)-(5)]

The enclosing theorem's other conclusions are ||Delta A_k||_2 <= c_1(m,k)||A_k||_2 epsilon_M, ||E_k||_2 <= c_2(m,k)||A_k||_2^2 epsilon_M, ||R_k||_2 = ||A_k||_2(1+mu_k) with |mu_k| <= c_3(m,k)epsilon_M, and ||Q_k||_2 <= sqrt(2). [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equations (4)-(6) and (8)]

In the proof, Q_k = (A_k + Delta A_k)R_k^(-1) follows exactly from equation (4), and the displayed congruence identity propagates equations (4)-(5) into the orthogonality estimate. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof of equation (7)]
implicit_context: All matrices are real, so the paper uses ordinary transpose rather than conjugate transpose. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: A in R^(m x n) and factorization notation]
The identity in equation (7) is printed as I without a subscript; its k x k dimension is forced by Q_k^T Q_k. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (7)]

A_k denotes exact input data, whereas Q_k and R_k are explicitly described as computed matrices; the paper uses no hats to distinguish computed quantities. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1 statement]
The restriction (3) is stated to assure that R is nonsingular and that equations (7) and (8) hold. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: paragraph following Theorem 1]
statement.algorithm_linkage: The result is specifically linked to CGS-P, not standard CGS-S. For k >= 2, CGS-P forms s_k = Q_(k-1)^T a_k and v_k = a_k - Q_(k-1)s_k, then uses psi_k = ||a_k||_2, phi_k = ||s_k||_2, and the pythagorean diagonal r_kk = (psi_k - phi_k)^(1/2)(psi_k + phi_k)^(1/2), followed by q_k = v_k/r_kk. Standard CGS-S instead uses r_kk = ||v_k||_2, and the paper says no bound such as (7) is guaranteed for that variant. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: Algorithm 1 and distinction from Algorithm 2; PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2; PDF p. 8, printed p. 306, anchor: Conclusion]
numerical_model: The explicit model is fl(x+y) = (x+y)(1+delta), with |delta| <= epsilon_M, for results in the normalized range. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: IEEE floating-point model]

For a modest function p(n), the paper uses (1+epsilon_M)^(p(n)) = 1+p(n)epsilon_M+O(epsilon_M^2) and assumes the second-order contribution is insignificant. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: linear approximation]

The appendix explicitly models psi_k = fl(||a_k||_2) and phi_k = fl(||s_k||_2), each with relative error bounded by (0.5m+1)epsilon_M + O(epsilon_M^2). [PDF p. 9, printed p. 307, anchor: equations (14)-(15)]
No particular binary precision is fixed; epsilon_M remains the generic machine unit. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: floating-point model and statement preceding Lemma 1]
error_notions: The selected error notion is loss of left orthogonality, measured by ||I - Q_k^T Q_k||_2. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (7)]

The proof also uses the factorization residual Delta A_k = Q_kR_k - A_k and the normal-equations error E_k = R_k^T R_k - A_k^T A_k. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equations (4)-(5); PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof of equation (7)]
The selected bound is absolute in ||I - Q_k^T Q_k||_2; it is not normalized by ||Q_k||_2 or by a dimension factor. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (7)]
norms: The paper consistently writes ||.||_2. In dimensional context this is the Euclidean norm for vectors and the induced spectral 2-norm for matrices. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: Algorithm 1 vector norms; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: kappa_2 definition and equation (7)]

The condition number in both the hypothesis and conclusion is the 2-norm condition number of the computed triangular prefix R_k. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: definition of kappa_2(R_k), equations (3) and (7)]
constants_and_indexing: For k = 1, c_1(m,1) = 1 and c_2(m,1) = m+2. For k = 2,...,n, c_1(m,k) = 2 sqrt(2) m k + 2 sqrt(k), and c_2(m,k) = 3.5 m k^2 - 1.5 m k + 16k. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2)]
c_3(m,k) = 0.5 c_2(m,k), and the constant in the selected result is exactly c_4(m,k) = c_2(m,k) + 2c_1(m,k). [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2)]
Both hypothesis (3) and conclusion (7) contain the square kappa_2(R_k)^2, not an unsquared condition number. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equations (3) and (7)]
The hypothesis and conclusion range over every prefix index k = 1,...,n; they are not stated only for k = n. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1]
higher_order_terms: Theorem 1 qualifies all displayed conclusions (4)-(8) by saying they hold to within terms of O(epsilon_M^2). [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: sentence introducing equations (4)-(8)]

Equation (7) is displayed without an explicit additive O(epsilon_M^2), but its appendix derivation ends with c_4(m,k)kappa_2(R_k)^2 epsilon_M + O(epsilon_M^2). [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (7); PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: final estimate proving equation (7)]

The paper supplies no explicit coefficient or uniform dependence for the suppressed O(epsilon_M^2) term. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: first-order convention; PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof estimate]
exceptional_values: The displayed IEEE relative-error formula is restricted to results in the normalized range. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: floating-point model]

Under condition (3), the appendix concludes that R is nonsingular, r_kk > 0, and hence psi_k > phi_k for Algorithm 2's real square-root computation. [PDF p. 9, printed p. 307, anchor: Lemma 2 proof following equations (14)-(15)]
Outside Theorem 1's assumptions, phi_k >= psi_k can cause Algorithm 2 to break down and return non-real Q and R. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 305, anchor: Remark 2]

The cited model does not separately specify handling of overflow, underflow, subnormal results, infinities, or NaNs beyond its normalized-range qualification. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: floating-point model]

undebatable_constraints: The input is a real m x n matrix with m >= n and inherited full-column-rank assumption rank(A) = n. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: standing rectangular full-rank setup]
The algorithm variant is CGS-P with the pythagorean diagonal formula, not standard CGS-S and not a reorthogonalized variant. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2]
Condition c_4(m,k)epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1 is required for every k. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (3)]
The selected conclusion holds for every prefix k = 1,...,n, not merely for the final Q and R. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (7)]
The left-hand side is exactly ||I - Q_k^T Q_k||_2. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equation (7)]

The right-hand side is exactly c_4(m,k)epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2, with c_4 = c_2 + 2c_1 and the piecewise c_1,c_2 definitions from equation (2). [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2) and equation (7)]
The condition number is that of the computed R_k, not directly that of A_k. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: kappa_2 definition and Remark 1]
The result is first-order and suppresses terms of O(epsilon_M^2). [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: linear approximation; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1 qualification]

ambiguities.issue: The theorem's condition uses kappa_2(R_k) = ||R_k||_2||R_k^(-1)||_2 before the following prose says that the condition assures R is nonsingular. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: definition of kappa_2, equation (3), and paragraph after Theorem 1]
ambiguities.evidence: The inverse-based definition precedes equation (3), while the post-theorem paragraph says restriction (3) assures nonsingularity. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: text surrounding Theorem 1]
ambiguities.impact: A formalization must either assume each R_k is invertible when stating the condition or define the condition number of a singular matrix as an extended value.

ambiguities.issue: The exact scope and coefficient of the suppressed O(epsilon_M^2) terms are not specified. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: linear approximation; PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1 qualification]
ambiguities.evidence: The paper only says p(n) is modest and that O(epsilon_M^2) makes no significant contribution; the proof retains an unquantified O(epsilon_M^2). [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: first-order convention; PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof of equation (7)]
ambiguities.impact: The source supports a first-order statement but does not determine an exact finite-epsilon remainder bound.

ambiguities.issue: The displayed rounding model explicitly covers addition and normalized-range results, while Algorithm 2 also uses norms, products, division, subtraction, and square roots. [PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2 and IEEE model]
ambiguities.evidence: The appendix later invokes computed-norm and standard error bounds, but the selected passages do not give a complete operation-by-operation IEEE semantics. [PDF p. 9, printed p. 307, anchor: equations (14)-(15)]
ambiguities.impact: A mechanized numerical model must add standard rounding assumptions that the paper leaves implicit, without strengthening the stated theorem beyond first order.

ambiguities.issue: The paper uses undecorated symbols for computed quantities. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1 statement]
ambiguities.evidence: The theorem calls Q_k and R_k computed matrices but writes them without hats; the appendix explicitly applies fl only when exposing individual computed operations such as psi_k and phi_k. [PDF p. 9, printed p. 307, anchor: equations (14)-(15)]
ambiguities.impact: A formalization must distinguish exact input A_k, computed Q_k and R_k, and exact residual definitions even though the paper's typography does not.

ambiguities.issue: The proof of equation (6) prints 1+c_3(m,k)epsilon_M+O(epsilon_M^2) = sqrt(1+c_2(m,k)), apparently omitting epsilon_M inside the square root. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof of equation (6)]
ambiguities.evidence: The theorem separately and unambiguously defines c_3 = 0.5c_2 and states equation (6), while the displayed proof line lacks epsilon_M under the radical. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: equation (2) and equation (6); PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof of equation (6)]
ambiguities.impact: This appears to be a typographical inconsistency in a companion result; it does not alter the explicit selected equation (7) or its direct proof using c_1 and c_2.

ambiguities.issue: The theorem speaks of R resulting from Algorithm 2, although Algorithm 2 can fail to produce real matrices when its square-root factors are invalid. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1; PDF p. 7, printed p. 305, anchor: Remark 2]
ambiguities.evidence: Remark 2 records breakdown when phi_k >= psi_k, while the appendix derives psi_k > phi_k under condition (3) after referring to the resulting R. [PDF p. 7, printed p. 305, anchor: Remark 2; PDF p. 9, printed p. 307, anchor: Lemma 2 proof]
ambiguities.impact: The statement can be read as conditional on successful real execution, or as asserting that condition (3) excludes breakdown; the paper does not formalize the algorithm's partiality.

contract_plain_english: Let A be a real m x n full-column-rank matrix with m >= n, and compute its prefixes Q_k and R_k using the pythagorean classical Gram-Schmidt Algorithm 2 in IEEE floating-point arithmetic. [PDF p. 2, printed p. 300, anchor: standing setup; PDF p. 3, printed p. 301, anchor: Algorithm 2] If every computed triangular prefix satisfies c_4(m,k)epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2 < 1, then, for every k = 1,...,n and after neglecting O(epsilon_M^2), the spectral-norm loss of column orthogonality obeys ||I_k - Q_k^T Q_k||_2 <= c_4(m,k)epsilon_M kappa_2(R_k)^2. [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: Theorem 1, equations (3) and (7)] Here kappa_2(R_k) = ||R_k||_2||R_k^(-1)||_2 and c_4 = c_2 + 2c_1 with the piecewise constants in equation (2). [PDF p. 4, printed p. 302, anchor: definitions preceding Theorem 1] The appendix derives the estimate from the factorization-residual and normal-equations bounds through an exact congruence identity, retaining an unquantified O(epsilon_M^2) remainder before applying the paper's first-order convention. [PDF p. 14, printed p. 312, anchor: proof of equation (7)]
